title: By what smallest number do we multiply 9408 to get a perfect square?
description: The primes of nine thousand four hundred eight are paired, and the prime without a partner decides the multiplier. The answer is put back by finding the square root and multiplying it by itself.
teaching_notes: One idea: give the lonely prime a partner by multiplying, and nothing more. Watch for students who multiply by a larger number, or who pair the sevens but forget the three.

video_script.why: The child uses the pairing of primes from the solved example to find the multiplier that makes a perfect square.
video_script.substitution: Write the number as primes, find the prime without a partner and multiply by it.
video_script.anchor: the number nine thousand four hundred eight on a card
video_script.payoff_line: Multiply by three, and the square root is one hundred sixty eight

final_answer.value: Multiply by 3; the product 28224 has square root 168
final_answer.spoken: multiply by three, and the square root of the new number is one hundred sixty eight

video_script.design: One idea: the prime without a partner gives the multiplier. The number card stays in the anchor band and the prime lines sit on the working board.

<bookmark mark='ask'/>By what smallest number must we multiply it to make a perfect square?

narration: <bookmark mark='pairs'/>In a perfect square, every prime has a partner.
<bookmark mark='left'/>We look for the prime that is alone, and give it a partner.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the number is nine thousand four hundred eight.

beats.on_screen: To find: the smallest multiplier that makes a perfect square, and the square root of the new number

marks.find: the thing to find is written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the smallest multiplier, and then the square root of the new number.

marks.pf: the words prime factorisation are written
marks.list: 9408 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 × 7 is written, one prime at a time

narration: <bookmark mark='pf'/>Step one, write nine thousand four hundred eight as primes.
<bookmark mark='list'/>It is six twos, then one three, then two sevens.

beats.on_screen: the six 2s join in three pairs, the two 7s join in one pair, and the single 3 stays outside in the warning colour

marks.pairs: the 2s and the 7s join in pairs
marks.alone: the single 3 stays outside and flashes

narration: <bookmark mark='pairs'/>Step two, look for partners.
The six twos make three pairs, and the two sevens make one pair.
<bookmark mark='alone'/>The three is alone.

beats.on_screen: 9408 × 3 = 28224 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 7 × 7; now every prime has a partner

marks.all: the new line shows every prime in a pair

narration: <bookmark mark='times'/>Step three, multiply by three to give the three a partner.
Nine thousand four hundred eight times three is twenty eight thousand two hundred twenty four.
<bookmark mark='all'/>Every prime in the new number now has a partner.

beats.on_screen: put the answer back: one group is 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 168, and 168 × 168 = 28224

marks.group: one of the two equal groups of primes is lifted out and 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 168 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='group'/>Step four, put the answer back in the question.
One group is two times two times two times three times seven, which is one hundred sixty eight.
<bookmark mark='back'/>One hundred sixty eight times one hundred sixty eight is twenty eight thousand two hundred twenty four.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Multiply by three, and the square root is one hundred sixty eight.
